profiles.bio: If your plot requires characters to share a single brain cell, I will document it with page numbers.
Former literature TA. Annotating continuity errors and bloated dialogue since 2012.
Professional copyeditor with zero patience for purple prose and redundant adjectives.
Checking your deus ex machina and unresolved cliffhangers at the door.
Reading the five-star hype trains so your group chat does not have to.
Five stars = catastrophic failure. Keeping Badreads honest one receipt at a time.
Expected a character arc. Received a checklist of marketing tropes.
If there is an enemies-to-lovers knife to the throat, I am deducting two stars immediately.
Investigating why the internet lied to me about this New York Times bestseller.
Reading 400-page paperbacks on delayed cross-country flights with growing indignation.
Chapter 52 and nothing has happened. Calling the narrative authorities.
Performing autopsies on books that should have remained rough drafts.

roasts.hook: A five-star disaster disguised as a New York Times bestseller.
roasts.body: The Da Vinci Code relies on cardboard character tropes and pacing so sluggish it feels like reading a court transcript. The central premise is intriguing for exactly two chapters before collapsing under repetitive dialogue and manufactured drama.

roasts.hook: The plot holes in The Da Vinci Code could fit a freight train.
roasts.body: Every major conflict resolution in this book depends on characters making the least logical choice available to human cognition. The prose tries to be profound but ends up sounding like a motivational poster filtered through a thesaurus.

roasts.hook: I want those eight hours of my reading life returned with interest.
roasts.body: The ending feels rushed, unearned, and completely detached from the stakes established in the first half. An exercise in marketing hype completely overpowering basic editorial quality control.

roasts.hook: A thesaurus was brutally harmed in the making of this manuscript.
roasts.body: The phrase 'inner goddess' appears so many times doing backflips and pirouettes that I began to wonder if the author was being held hostage by a gymnastics metaphor. The dialogue reads like automated email replies from a spreadsheet.

roasts.hook: Ana Steele has the survival instincts of a cardboard box in a rainstorm.
roasts.body: The entire emotional conflict could be resolved by a twenty-second conversation or five minutes with an actual attorney. The contract scenes read like a terms-of-service agreement written in Comic Sans.

roasts.hook: Fifty shades of repetitive sentence structures.
roasts.body: Every interaction follows the same formula: lip biting, dark brooding, sudden contract revisions, and another mention of an iPod playlist from 2008. The editing team clearly clocked out by chapter four.

roasts.hook: Watching someone sleep without permission is not a romance; it is a felony.
roasts.body: Edward Cullen is a 104-year-old predator who hangs out in high school cafeteria parking lots driving a Volvo. Bella's only personality trait is stumbling over flat carpet and inhaling deeply.

roasts.hook: The Cullen family baseball game is the only scene with actual kinetic energy.
roasts.body: The rest of the book is three hundred pages of staring, describing jawlines as chiseled marble, and complaining about the rain in Forks. The pacing crawls like a frozen Volvo.

roasts.hook: A vampire that sparkles is where the mythology surrendered.
roasts.body: Generations of vampire folklore built on bloodlust and darkness, reduced to body glitter and high school biology lab seating assignments. Truly catastrophic execution.

roasts.hook: A fantasy war college with the administrative competence of a middle school sleepover.
roasts.body: Cadets are murdered in hallways between breakfast and tactical theory, yet nobody investigates because 'it's Basgiath.' The modern slang completely shatters whatever world-building was attempted.

roasts.hook: Xaden Riorson exists entirely to lean against doorframes and smirk darkly.
roasts.body: Every interaction between Violet and Xaden is an exercise in mutual refusal to communicate basic military intelligence while noticing shadow daggers and abs. 500 pages of vibes over plot.

roasts.hook: The dragons are the only rational beings in this entire institution.
roasts.body: The parapet sequence alone violates every law of military logistics and human resources. If your dragon academy kills 40% of its recruits before flight training, you lose the war.

roasts.hook: The manuscript inside the manuscript reads like shock-value fan fiction.
roasts.body: Every twist in this book relies on characters making the most morally deranged and illogical decisions imaginable. The manuscript within the story is cartoonishly evil to the point of comedy.

roasts.hook: The final letter twist undoes whatever internal logic was left.
roasts.body: You cannot write a 250-page confessional of sociopathic behavior and then say 'just kidding, it was a writing exercise' in a two-page letter. That is not a twist; it is literary arson.

roasts.hook: Lowen is supposedly a professional author, yet acts like an intruder in a soap opera.
roasts.body: She snoops in drawers, makes terrible romantic choices with her employer within forty-eight hours, and ignores glaring red flags the size of billboards. Not a single receipt holds up.
